newsitem.title: USA: Conrail deal enters information blackout.
newsitem.headline: Conrail deal enters information blackout.

text.p: The takeover battle for Conrail Inc. was hidden in a black hole Monday, with the railroads involved sticking by their pledge not to discuss the progress of talks and analysts reduced to reading tea leaves.

Analysts said the few scraps of information available had both positive and negative ramifications for ending the deadlock between, on one side, intended merger partners Conrail and CSX Corp. and hostile suitor Norfolk Southern Corp. on the other side.
"We're probably both looking at the same tea cup, but I don't see any early movement," said PNC Bank analyst Charles Vincent.
"Conrail's got itself in a nasty position," he said.
Norfolk Southern is bidding $10.3 billion in cash for Conrail, whose cash-and-stock merger plan with CSX is valued at about $9.5 billion.
After a closely guarded meeting Friday, the chiefs of all three railroads said in a statement they would not discuss Friday's meeting or future talks on the deal.

Separately, Conrail said later in the day it had scheduled its annual meeting, normally held in May, for Dec. 19, 1997, and will in the meantime "devote its energies" to winning approval of the deal from shareholders -- who rejected it last month -- and federal regulators.

Although Friday's statement from the three railroads left open the door to future meetings, it did not specify that any had been planned. Norfolk Southern spokesman Bob Fort said he could not comment on the issue.
He said the blackout had been mutually agreed on, and was unrelated to the issue of any confidentiality agreement covering the deal.
Conrail and CSX representatives also either declined to comment or said they had no information.
Vincent said the apparent willingness to hold additional talks, and even the news blackout itself, was positive. But he saw no signs of an imminent deal.
"It indicates to me that probably some movement has taken place," Vincent said.

But DLJ Securities analyst James Higgins said Conrail's late scheduling of its annual meeting -- and the announcement of the change on the same day as the talks -- seemed a gesture of defiance reflecting a continued stalemate.
"I just don't think Conrail would have gone out of its way to set a very late meeting date on the day of this first meeting if it thought things were going well," Higgins said. "It's ticklish."
Norfolk Southern has previously said it would try to unseat Conrail's board of directors at the annual meeting.

While the blackout continues, opportunities for new public information on the deal include a Feb. 25 federal appeals court hearing in Philadelphia, at which Norfolk Southern will seek to overturn lower-court denials of its legal challenge to the merger, and filings of rival merger plans before federal regulators in March.
A Norfolk Southern attorney said the railroad is proceeding with its legal case, but Higgins said he did not believe the courts would significantly alter the deal.
PNC Bank's Vincent said Conrail's position appears to be increasingly squeezed and said the likelihood the railroad will be split up between its two suitors looms large.
Although Conrail dramatically failed to win shareholder approval of a key provision that would have allowed the CSX deal to go forward, CSX appears unwilling to raise its bid, he said.

Conrail's strongest leverage is the two-year "lockout" provision in its deal with CSX which prevents either company from discussing a deal with a third party until 1999 without mutual approval, Vincent said.

"The only thing it (Conrail) can do is impress upon its shareholders that they're not going to get anything at all until the lockout period is over if they persist in supporting Norfolk Southern," he said.
